summaries.example: Imagine that someone wrote down yesterday exactly what choice you will make tomorrow, and that this person cannot ever be wrong. Can you choose differently tomorrow? One side says no: the old writing is already fixed, and it must be correct. Another side says yes: your choice is still your own, and the writing is correct because it records what you will freely do. The puzzle is about whether knowing a choice makes the choice happen.
summaries.summary:
This entry examines a puzzle about two ideas: an all-knowing being may know every future choice, while people may still have free will. The argument for theological fatalism begins with a simple thought. Suppose a perfect knower believed yesterday that you will answer a phone tomorrow. Yesterday is over, so you cannot change that belief. Because the belief cannot be mistaken, you also cannot make it false. It seems to follow that you cannot do anything except answer the phone. If being free requires being able to do otherwise, then the action was not free.

Philosophers disagree about which step causes trouble. Compatibilists think perfect foreknowledge and free will can fit together. They may deny that every future choice is already true, explain how an all-knowing being relates to time, say that a past belief about the future is not an ordinary fixed past fact, or argue that the future action explains the belief rather than the belief forcing the action. Some challenge the idea that freedom always requires another available choice. Incompatibilists think the two ideas cannot both remain in their strongest forms, so they reject perfect foreknowledge, libertarian free will, or both.

The discussion is not only about religion. It also asks whether the past is fixed in every relevant way, how truth works for future events, and whether necessity must be understood as a kind of force. Similar questions appear in logical fatalism and in debates about determinism.
key_ideas: The central puzzle asks whether perfect knowledge of the future leaves people free.
The argument says the past cannot be changed, and a perfect prediction cannot be false. So, it seems, the predicted action cannot be avoided.
Some philosophers think the argument has a mistaken step. They suggest that future statements may not yet be true, that God may not be in time, or that past beliefs about the future are special.
Other philosophers give up either perfect future knowledge or the strongest kind of free will.
The puzzle also raises wider questions about time, truth, and what it means for something to be necessary.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue helps us think carefully about choice and responsibility. It shows that a fact about what will happen is not automatically a cause of what happens. It also teaches an important philosophical habit: when an argument seems convincing, examine each step instead of accepting or rejecting the whole argument at once.

important_terms.definition: Knowing something before it happens.
The idea that a person can make a choice and could have chosen another way.
The view that events must happen in one way and cannot happen differently.
A belief that cannot be wrong.
A choice or event that could happen but could also happen another way.

questions_to_think_about: If a prediction cannot be wrong, does it cause your choice, or does it simply describe it?
Can you be responsible for an action if you could not have done something else?
Are statements about tomorrow already true today?
Does knowing what someone will do make that person do it?

summaries.example: Suppose an infallible being believed yesterday that you will answer a phone at 9:00 tomorrow. The basic argument says: the past is now necessary; therefore yesterday's belief is now necessary; necessarily, an infallible belief entails that you answer; necessity transfers through that entailment; so your answering is now unavoidable. If free action requires the ability to do otherwise, your answering is not free. A compatibilist may instead say that the future action explains why the belief is correct, or that inability to do otherwise does not by itself remove responsibility.
summaries.summary:
The entry studies whether infallible foreknowledge is compatible with libertarian free will. The core argument can be represented with a future action such as answering a phone. If an infallible being believed yesterday that the action would occur, then, according to the Principle of the Necessity of the Past, that past belief is now fixed. Since infallibility means the belief cannot be false, and since necessity is assumed to transfer through entailment, the future action becomes fixed as well. The final step invokes the Principle of Alternate Possibilities: if the agent cannot do otherwise, the action is not free.

The argument is generally regarded as valid in form, so compatibilists must reject a premise or deny that the conclusion about unfreedom follows. One response denies that contingent propositions about the future already have truth values. Another accepts future truth but questions how such truths could be known infallibly. The eternity solution says that God does not believe at an earlier time; instead, a timeless God apprehends all events without occupying a temporal position. Ockhamist approaches distinguish hard past facts from soft past facts, suggesting that a past divine belief about a future act is not fixed in exactly the same way as an ordinary past event. Dependence theories add that the belief is explanatorily dependent on the future act, not a cause of it. Other proposals question the transfer of necessity or reject PAP, sometimes using Frankfurt-style cases in which an agent seems responsible despite lacking alternatives.

Incompatibilist responses give up one of the two commitments. Open-theist views reject infallible exhaustive foreknowledge, while other views reject libertarian freedom. The entry also compares theological fatalism with older
key_ideas: The formal fatalist argument is often treated as valid if its premises are accepted; the main dispute concerns premises about the past, necessity transfer, and freedom.
Ordinary human foreknowledge is fallible. The distinctive problem concerns infallible belief, not merely accurate prediction supported by evidence.
Compatibilist responses target different premises: future contingent truth, God's temporal status, the necessity of the past, explanatory dependence, the transfer of necessity, or PAP.
The dependence approach holds that God's belief is correct because the future action occurs, while the action does not occur because God believed it would.
The eternity solution removes the claim that God believed at an earlier time, but critics ask whether a parallel argument can be made about timeless knowledge.
Some incompatibilists retain libertarian freedom by rejecting infallible foreknowledge; others reject libertarian freedom while allowing a weaker, compatibilist kind of freedom.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate separates several ideas that are easily confused: knowing, causing, determining, explaining, and preventing. It also tests whether the past is fixed in an absolute way, whether truth about the future works like truth about the past, and whether responsibility requires alternatives. These distinctions matter in philosophy of religion, metaphysics, theories of time, and debates about free will.

important_terms.definition: The thesis that infallible knowledge of a future act makes that act necessary and therefore unfree.
A strong view of free will according to which an agent has genuine alternatives and is not determined in the relevant sense.
The idea that a past event has a special necessity because no one can now alter or prevent it.
The principle that an action is free only if the agent could have done otherwise.
A fact about the past that is partly connected to, or depends on, how the future turns out.
A relation in which one fact is explained by another; some theories say divine foreknowledge depends on the future act, not vice versa.
The view that God is not located at a moment in time but grasps all temporal events in an atemporal present.
A theory that includes God's knowledge of truths about what any free creature would do in possible circumstances.

questions_to_think_about: Does the fact that an event is entailed by an infallible past belief make the event unavoidable, or does the entailment run in an explanatory direction that matters?
Can a past belief about the future be as fixed as an ordinary past event if its correctness depends on the future?
Must free will include the ability to do otherwise, or can an agent be free when alternatives are unavailable but the foreknowledge does not cause the action?
If future contingent propositions are not yet true, can an all-knowing being know them?
Is theological fatalism a special religious problem, or a version of a broader problem about time, necessity, and determinism?

summaries.example: Your friend says, “I knew yesterday that you would choose chocolate ice cream today.” The friend could have been mistaken, so the knowledge did not force your choice. Now change the story: imagine the friend is never wrong. One thinker says that because the perfect belief already existed, you cannot choose vanilla. Another says your choice is still free because the belief is right by describing what you choose, not by pushing you to choose it. Philosophers debate whether the perfect-belief case is really like the ordinary case.
summaries.summary:
This entry explores a famous question: if a being knows every future choice without any chance of being wrong, can people still choose freely? The argument for theological fatalism uses a phone-call example. Suppose a perfect knower believed yesterday that you will answer tomorrow. You cannot change yesterday, and the belief cannot turn out false. It may seem that you therefore cannot do anything except answer. If freedom requires the power to do otherwise, your answer would not be free.

Philosophers who think the two ideas can fit together are called compatibilists. They challenge different parts of the argument. Some deny that statements about undetermined future events are already true. Others accept such truths but ask how an infallible being could know them. A different proposal says God is eternal rather than located in time, so God does not first believe something yesterday and then wait for it to happen. Another proposal distinguishes ordinary fixed facts about the past from “soft” facts that include a connection to the future. On this view, a past divine belief may depend on the future event in a special way. Dependence theorists emphasize that the future act explains why the belief is correct, not that the belief causes the act. Some philosophers also question whether necessity can be passed from a past belief to everything it implies, or whether freedom always requires another possible action.

Incompatibilists accept that perfect foreknowledge and libertarian freedom cannot both remain. They may reject infallible foreknowledge, as in open-future approaches, or reject libertarian freedom while keeping a different account of freedom. The entry connects this debate with logical fatalism and broader questions about time and necessity.
key_ideas: The puzzle is specifically about infallible foreknowledge, not ordinary guesses or well-supported predictions.
The main argument moves from a fixed past belief to a future action and then says the action cannot be avoided.
Compatibilists look for a false step. They may question future truth, the necessity of the past, the way necessity transfers, or the need for alternatives.
Some philosophers say God is outside time, so it is misleading to say God believed something yesterday.
Other philosophers say a past belief about a future act is a special kind of past fact because it depends on how the future turns out.
Incompatibilists give up either infallible foreknowledge or libertarian free will.
summaries.why_it_matters: The question matters because it affects how we understand choice, responsibility, prediction, and time. It also shows why philosophical arguments need careful definitions. “Knowing,” “causing,” and “forcing” may sound similar in everyday speech, but the debate depends on keeping them separate.

important_terms.definition: Knowing in advance that something will happen.
The power to make a choice, often understood as being able to choose among real alternatives.
The claim that events, including human actions, must happen in one fixed way.
A belief that cannot be false.
A statement about a future event that might happen but might also not happen.
The idea that what has already happened cannot now be changed.
The rule that freedom requires the ability to do something else.
The view that perfect foreknowledge and a strong kind of free will can exist together.

questions_to_think_about: Does a perfect prediction make an event happen, or can it be correct without causing it?
Is a future choice already true before it happens?
Could a person be responsible even if no other choice was possible?
Is a belief from the past always fixed in the same way as a past physical event?
Which would be harder to give up: perfect knowledge of the future or the strongest kind of free will?
